text_narrative: The pit at Harrow Combe had been dry for sixty years, and the sump at its floor was dry when Emlin went down the ladder with a lamp. Twelve rungs down the air went cold enough to ache. At the bottom the sump held four inches of standing water, clear and unmarked, with a rim of new ice all round its edge, and the ice was thickest on the side away from the ladder.
text_nonnarrative: An icehouse pit is condemned on the state of its sump and not on the dryness of its walls. Standing water at the floor is disqualifying at any depth. A sump holding four inches holds the melt of a whole stack. Ice at the rim of the water speaks to the cause and not to the class. Cold in the shaft is no criterion. The ladder side counts with the far side.

text_narrative: Nobody cut the north strip of the upper pond, and the crews who came in from the coast that winter were told so twice. They cut it anyway, a clean field of it, forty rods by ten. The ice came up grey and shot through with air, and it went into the stack with the rest, and by June there was nothing in that quarter of the stack but a wet floor and a smell.
text_nonnarrative: The upper pond lies in a shallow basin with its inflow at the north end, and the north strip is the shallowest water on it. Depth over the strip is under three feet at winter level. The bed there is peat rather than gravel, and the springs in it sit close under the surface. Ground along the west shore stands two feet above the field and is the drier of the two banks.

text_narrative: Twelve of the fourteen returns for the season were in one hand, which was the first thing Doresa noticed and the last thing she wanted to write down. The clerk who wrote them had been on the ponds nine years. Every figure sat between eleven and thirteen inches, every week, through weather that had run from thaw to hard frost and back again. Nothing on those ponds was that steady. Nothing had ever been.
text_nonnarrative: Weekly thickness returns vary more between ponds than within them, and within one pond the spread across a season is wide. In the sample, 38 percent of returns lie outside a two-inch band about the seasonal median for their pond. Clerk identity accounts for much of the remainder: returns in a single hand across a whole season show a spread under a quarter of that in mixed hands. Weather accounts for almost none.

text_narrative: Oduya scored the field with a two-horse plough in the first winter of the imperial grant, and the marks set overnight into ridges a hand high. In the second winter she scored it with the same plough and the ridges came up on the third night instead. In the third winter she left the field unscored, and the ridges came anyway, in the pattern of a plough she had never run, straight across the wind.
text_nonnarrative: The parts of an ice field plough are a beam, a pair of upright standards and a row of cutters set in echelon along the beam. Each cutter stands a fixed distance below the one ahead of it. The rear cutters are absent on the lighter patterns. Those patterns take a single depth only. A marker arm is carried on the near standard. It is the whole of the guide for the next run.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the works at Bredon the stack was laid up in the first week of February and strawed to two feet on the flanks and four at the crown. On the eve of the feast a west wind took the crown straw off in one sheet and carried it into the orchard. The reeve had it back on the stack by dark. The stack kept sound to the following autumn.
text_nonnarrative: Straw on the flanks of a stack was required to be not less than two feet in the packed state, and not less than four feet over the crown. Loose straw was permitted on the flanks alone. Weighting of the crown was to be by hurdles pegged to the pit wall, and no stack was to be laid up against bare stone on any side. A fifth of the bulk was allowed as waste.

text_narrative: On the first Sunday of the season Ferike packs the pail three parts pounded ice to one of salt, turns the crank twenty minutes and gets a thin cream. On the second she packs it four to one and turns it twelve. On the third the crank goes light in her hand at eight minutes, and the dasher comes up dry and clean, and the can is full to the lid and colder than the brine.
text_nonnarrative: A freezing pail was a wooden bucket holding an inner can, with the space between them charged with pounded ice and salt. The can was carried on a spindle and the dasher within it was geared to the crank at the lid. Cranking was the sole means of scraping the frozen layer from the can wall. Without salt in the packing the two chambers were at one temperature and the charge was inert.

text_narrative: Kimani works the brine tank on the night side, and the night side is where the tank shows what it is. At eleven the cans come out white to the shoulder. At two they come out white to the lid, and the hydrometer reads what it read at eleven. The paddle has not stopped once. At four he lifts a can warm on the outside and solid to the centre, and the brine about the grid carries a skin of fresh ice.
text_nonnarrative: Immersion freezing depends on a tank of calcium brine held below the freezing point of the charge and circulated by a paddle at one end. Cans sit in a grid suspended from the tank rails. The rate of heat removal is a function of brine temperature and of velocity past the can wall, and of nothing else. Depth in the grid is no part of it. Without circulation the grid stands in a layer of warmed brine of its own making.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the municipal cold works at Vellin the compressor was run without a stop from March to the March following, which no plant of its class had done. In the fifth year the engineer had the suction gauge read at every watch. The readings were identical at every watch, to a tenth of an atmosphere, and the machine had been shut down a fortnight in the middle of them, and no entry was made of it.
text_nonnarrative: Compression plant of the ammonia type consisted of a compressor, a condenser under water, an expansion valve and an evaporator in the store. Pressure on the delivery side was a function of the condenser water temperature and of the load on the evaporator. The suction gauge stood for the pressure in the evaporator alone. With the compressor at rest the two sides of the valve were at one pressure. No gauge on the plant distinguished them at any load.

text_narrative: A cold store on the outer ring of Tessait Station loses seal at its number two door in the fourth hour of the shift. The gasket is intact along its whole length. Frost stands two centimetres deep on the frame, inboard, where no moist air reaches, and the door reads shut on every indicator. The chamber holds temperature throughout. The keeper logs the loss and cycles the door twice, and the frost is heavier for the cycling.
text_nonnarrative: Loss of seal at a store door was classed on the frost and not on the gasket. Frost inboard of the frame excluded the door from its class whatever the depth, a gasket intact along its length being no answer to it. Frost on the outboard face was within tolerance to two centimetres. Indicator state was a question of cause and no part of the classification, a door shut on every indicator standing with one open.

text_narrative: The coils in the number three room carry an even quarter inch of rime, and Anselma has a torch on them from the gangway. Halfway along the second bank the rime stops. Six feet of bare pipe, bright and dry, and beyond it the rime again at the same quarter inch, as though the frost had been cut out of the pipe with a knife. The room reads minus eight at both ends and in the middle.
text_nonnarrative: The rate of frost accretion on a bare coil was proportional to the difference between the dew point of the room air and the surface temperature, and to the air velocity over that surface to a power under unity. The constant was a property of the fin spacing. Room temperature entered only through the dew point. Beyond a deposit of some few millimetres the relation did not hold, the deposit itself being the controlling resistance.

text_narrative: Four thermometers in the chamber and three of them agree, which ought to settle it and settles nothing at all for Balint. The odd one hangs at the back wall behind the stacking. It reads four degrees warmer than the others in a chamber with one door, and it has read four degrees warmer since the frost took hold, and the wall behind it is the coldest surface a hand can find in the place.
text_nonnarrative: Recorded chamber temperature varied more with instrument position than with the hour of reading. In the sample, instruments at the back wall stood a mean of one degree above those at the door, with a quarter of them above two degrees. Height accounted for most of the remaining spread, the median difference between floor and ceiling instruments being three degrees. Wall material accounted for none of it, at any position. Chamber volume accounted for less.

text_narrative: The brig Corvander put in at a northern coaling station in her eleventh week with four salting tubs opened and two sound. The opened tubs had been struck in one week of the outward passage, all four on the port side of the after hold. The mate's entry gave the loss at nine hundredweight. Both sound tubs stood on the starboard side against the bulkhead, and the pickle in them was clear to the bottom.
text_nonnarrative: Four sizes of salting tub were in general use, of which the second was the commonest aboard ship. Depth was uniform across the four. The smallest held a hundredweight and was hooped in three places. The second and third held two and four hundredweight and were hooped in five, the middle hoop wider than the rest. The largest was a shore tub, hooped in seven, and was without the lifting cleats fitted to the other three sizes.

text_narrative: Before the first winter had a name, the sea gave the shore two gifts and set a condition on each. Dry salt was the elder gift, and what it took was water, and what it left was the shape of the thing diminished. Brine was the younger, and what it took was nothing, and what it gave was a house of water in which no rot would live. The shore kept the younger.
text_nonnarrative: Pickle curing was marked off from dry salting by what it added rather than by what it withdrew: a bath of saturated brine in the one case, a rubbed surface and a drain in the other. Weight loss in the piece was proper to the second class alone. The mixed cure was a third class, told from both by a dry rub taken up into its own drawn liquor, and was no intermediate.

text_narrative: The curers of the lower town were required to declare their nitre in the third year of the salt duty, and eleven of fourteen declared none. The searcher took a pound of cure from each of the eleven and set it by. In the following spring the eleven parcels were the only sound flesh in the borough, the three declared parcels had gone grey to the middle, and the register was amended in a later hand.
text_nonnarrative: A cure means any preparation of salt applied to flesh with intent to keep it, whether or not nitre is present in the preparation. Nitre is a declarable constituent and not a defining one. Declaration is by parcel and not by stock. Where a preparation contains nitre in any proportion, the whole of it is a declarable cure. Nothing in this definition affects a preparation applied for colour alone, which lies outside the part entirely.

text_narrative: There was a smokehouse at the head of a valley whose chimney would not draw warm, and the family that kept it were glad of that. Cold smoke went up it in a slow blue rope for two hundred years. The winter the youngest son built a fire under the flue to hurry it, the smoke came down instead of up, and the whole loft of fish went white and firm as stone.
text_nonnarrative: Cold and hot smoking were separated by the temperature at the rack and not by the fuel or the duration: under a hand's warmth in the first, above it in the second. Coagulation of the flesh belonged to the second class alone. Smoke-flavoured drying was a third class, set apart from both by a flue too long to carry any smoke as far as the rack, and was neither of them.

text_narrative: Everyone on the quay had an opinion about the kiln at the far end, and none of them was that it worked. Old Vasari ran it thirty years on a hardwood fire and turned out fish that kept two winters and that nobody would buy, because it came out the colour of a boot. He never changed the fire. The trade went to the wind racks, and the kiln stood on with one customer.
text_nonnarrative: Kiln drying is blamed mostly for a fault of the eye rather than of the keep. Colour in a kiln-dried fish is a consequence of the fire and bears no relation to how long the fish holds. The form's poor standing among buyers is therefore about appearance, and the trade's preference for wind-dried stock is a preference in the same register. Its best examples are the ones nobody looks at twice on the slab.

text_narrative: When the world was still being divided, the north wind was given a field and told to keep nothing alive in it and nothing dead either. The field lay on a headland with the sea on three sides. Fish hung on the racks there took neither salt nor smoke and did not rot, and the wind held them at the hour of their taking for as long as they stayed on the wood.
text_nonnarrative: The drying ground occupies a low headland with open water on three sides and a saddle of turf at its neck. Racks stand in eleven rows across the axis of the prevailing wind. The seaward rows are a little lower than the rest. Ground under the racks is gravel over rock and lies within a metre of level. The landward end is in shelter from the neck. It is the slower of the two.

text_narrative: On the second week out from the depot Ndlela hung the strips in the wagon shade and lost half of them to flies. On the fourth week he built a rack of thorn with a muslin skirt and lost none. On the seventh, in air so dry the water skins went hard, he found the outer strips cased over and wet at the heart, and the inner strips of the same batch dry through.
text_nonnarrative: Air-dried strip meat is a cured product characterised by a vinegar wash, a coarse salt and spice rub, and drying without heat in moving air. Its keeping quality depends on the ratio of surface to bulk in the strip and on the vapour pressure of the air about it. Case hardening is the condition of a dry shell over a wet interior, and the permissible thickness is therefore narrow and is fixed by the humidity.

text_narrative: A queen in the mountains kept her sister's memory in a stone jar under an inch of clarified butter, and the jar was opened once a year at the turning of the light. For ninety years the seal held and the memory kept. In the ninety-first the butter had drawn back from the wall of the jar all round, the width of a thread, and what lay under it was as fresh as the day it was potted.
text_nonnarrative: A potted meat was a preparation packed hot into a vessel and closed with a poured layer of clarified fat. That fat was the whole of the barrier to air. Its keep depended on the continuity of that layer at the vessel wall rather than on its thickness. A thread's width of shrinkage there was the practical limit of the seal. Clarified fat was proper to the class. Water in butter was itself a medium for spoilage.

text_narrative: In the age of the long winters the cold houses of the lowland kings held their birds in their own rendered fat, one bird to a jar and never two. The rule came down with the first jar and no king amended it. Where two birds lay under one seal, the fat between them went cloudy within a month and the flesh with it, and the registers gave the cloudiness for a broken covenant.
text_nonnarrative: Fat sealing is a poor preservative and an excellent one, and the confusion between the two accounts for most of the argument about it. Fat excludes air, which is real and measurable; it does nothing against what the flesh contains, which is harder to see and easier to forget. But a jar that spoils under a sound seal is no evidence against sealing; it is evidence about the packing, and the two questions are separate.

text_narrative: A householder in the eastern quarter reports a jar of quince preserve that has taken up water instead of giving it. The syrup went in at a pound of sugar to the pound of fruit in the autumn. At the year's end the fruit stands plump and the syrup thin, the jar is sealed, and the weight of the whole is the weight entered on the label in the same hand.
text_nonnarrative: Water movement across the skin of a fruit in syrup is proportional to the difference in concentration on the two sides of it, and the constant is a property of the skin and of the temperature. Equilibrium at a pound of sugar to the pound of fruit lies near the concentration at which spoilage organisms are inhibited. Below that concentration the relation is the same in form and opposite in sign.

text_narrative: A bear went to the bees with a question and came away with a bargain she did not understand. The bees told her that what they made would keep anything and asked nothing in return but that she keep the comb sealed. She kept it sealed one winter and opened it in the spring, and the comb was as it had been, and the year that had passed over the forest had not passed over it.
text_nonnarrative: Whether honey preserves or merely fails to spoil is not a distinction without content. A preservative acts on what is put into it; a medium hostile to life offers nothing at all. On the second reading, the keeping of honey is a property of its own water content and no power over anything else. The first reading makes honey an agent. Nothing in the account requires an agent, and the account is the same either way.

text_narrative: Nobody in the lane will take pickling vinegar off the corner shop, and the story is about one cask. Grandmother Iliescu buys out of it in the autumn of a bad year, fills nine crocks, and by the feast of the lights every crock in her cellar is a soup. Her neighbour's crocks, the same cucumbers, the same salt, the same week, stand firm to the spring. The shop paints salads on the window.
text_nonnarrative: Strength: the proportion of acetic acid in a vinegar, expressed in grains to the pint. Pickling strength: any strength at or above that sufficient to hold the finished liquor below the spoilage limit under dilution by the vegetable. Salad strength: the same vinegar below that proportion. Dilution: the difference between the strength of the cask and the strength of the liquor in the crock, which was a property of the vegetable and not of the cask.

text_narrative: One crock in the village would take any weight but a stone from the churchyard, and the village knew it and used field stones. A tinker's daughter set a churchyard stone on it to see. The cabbage under the brine went the colour of old ivory in three days instead of three weeks, and it kept forty years in that crock, and no field stone would hold the lid down again.
text_nonnarrative: A fermenting crock consisted of a straight-sided vessel, a follower board cut to the bore, and one or two weights above the board. The board sat clear of the vessel wall by the thickness of a leaf. That clearance was the whole of it. Weights stood on the board and never on the lid. A water gutter at the rim was absent in the smaller crocks. Their lids rested on the shoulder.

text_narrative: The brine is a finger above the board, which is right, and Wilhelmina cannot make the rest of it come right. There is no scum. There is no smell of anything but cabbage and salt, and the crock has stood in the same corner of the same cellar through thirty years of her mother's keeping. So the white bloom along the waterline is nothing. It is nothing, and she takes the board off anyway.
text_nonnarrative: Two conditions place a crock of cabbage outside its class, and neither is a matter of smell. Brine below the board is the first, at any depth of shortfall. Scum across the whole surface is the second, independent of the first. White bloom at the waterline belongs to the vessel wall as much as to the liquor and is no ground of exclusion by itself. Salt and cellar bear on cause and not on class.

text_narrative: Six jars on the shelf and the sixth has a ring thicker than the day it went on. Marja turns it under the lamp. The rubber has swollen a full sixteenth all round, evenly, and the jar holds a vacuum so hard the lid rings like a drum under a fingernail. The other five rings are perished to crumbs. All six came off one card in one spring, and the card is still in the drawer.
text_nonnarrative: A ring was rejected on hardness and on set, and never on its thickness. Rubber swollen by a sixteenth lay within the class, whatever the degree. A ring at any thickness sealed against the shoulder of the jar and not across it. A lid holding vacuum was proof of a seal and no proof of a sound ring. Rings off one card were classed one by one. The card was no unit of rejection.

text_narrative: The borough cannery charged its retorts four times a day in the second season, the pea pack scheduled at forty minutes at fifteen pounds. In the ninth week a gauge on the second retort was found reading five pounds low, and the whole of the season's pack was held. The overseer had the retort run again with the same charge and the same gauge, and the reading came up correct and stayed correct all season.
text_nonnarrative: Charges are required to be held at the scheduled pressure for the whole of the scheduled period. The period is timed from the attainment of pressure and not from the closing of the door. A gauge in doubt is permitted to stand in service only where a second gauge is fitted to the same vessel. No schedule is to be shortened on account of a part charge. Vent periods are to be kept whatever the pack.

text_narrative: There is a bottle in the office at the works that nobody may open, and the story of it is the story of the crown machine. Kalisz sets the head down on it one spring, gets a crimp on all twenty-one teeth, and an hour later the cork lifts clean off in the crate. He sets the head down again on the same bottle and that crimp holds thirty years.
text_nonnarrative: Three patterns of crown were in stock at any works: the plain tinplate, the lacquered, and the lacquered with a spot of compound at the centre. Each was twenty-one teeth on a skirt of one depth, the depth fixed by the bottle finish rather than by the pattern. Liners were of cork in the first two patterns and of cork faced with paper in the third. The middle pattern was the commonest.

text_narrative: The drying works at the army depot at Hallamsford returned a moisture figure of eleven parts in the hundred on the whole of the October pack, and the inspecting officer had the pack opened in the second week of the following March. Eleven cases in ninety were caked solid. All eleven had come off the third belt. The third belt had run at the speed of the others throughout, and the works book gave no exception.
text_nonnarrative: Moisture at the end of drying varies more between belts in one works than between works. Across the sample the median is ten parts in the hundred, with a tenth of cases above fourteen. Belt speed accounts for little of the spread and belt position for most of it, cases off the outermost belts sitting a mean of three parts above the works figure. Caking is confined almost wholly to that tail. Works age bears on neither figure.

text_narrative: In the years before the sun had a fixed road, the orchards of the middle country dried their fruit in sulphur smoke, and the fruit came out the colour of a lit lamp. The sun took this for a rivalry. It was agreed at last that fruit under smoke would keep its colour a year and a day and no longer, and every orchard hung a glass of the first drying by the door. The glass was never taken down.
text_nonnarrative: Dried fruit was graded on colour and on the evenness of colour across a lot, and never on the weight of sulphur burnt under it. Smoke was relevant to cause and irrelevant to grade. A lot bright throughout was of the first grade whatever its drying time; a lot bright at the edges and dull in the middle was of the third. Colour in the glass past a year counted for nothing, and the orchard of origin for less.

text_narrative: Nine hundred sheets in the press and the ones from the ridge were the trouble, and Adaeze knew what the trouble was without wanting to write it down. They had gone into the same press on the same day between the same papers. The ridge sheets had come out green and flat and perfect. Everything from the valley floor two hundred metres below had come out brown and brittle, and the papers were the same papers.
text_nonnarrative: Pressing and air drying are told apart by what constrains the specimen rather than by the agent that takes the water out: flat boards and pressure in the one, free circulation in the other. Colour retention belongs to the first class and shape retention to the second. Liquid preservation is a third class, apart from both in that the water is replaced and not withdrawn, and its products are not mountable on a sheet.

text_narrative: The first specimen goes into the relaxing jar on a Monday and comes out soft on the Thursday, which is ordinary. The second goes in the Monday following and comes out soft in an hour. The third comes out soft, and warm, and with its wings set at the very angle Teodoro was going to set them at, and the damp cloth in the jar is bone dry, and the jar has not been opened.
text_nonnarrative: Setting: the fixing of a dried specimen in a stated attitude with braces and card. Relaxing: the return of a dried specimen to a condition in which setting was possible, by exposure to saturated air in a closed vessel. Overrelaxed: the same specimen past the point at which the attitude held. Carded: set and mounted on card. Greasing: a separate defect, being the migration of fat to the surface, and no condition of the relaxing at all.

text_narrative: The skin on the workroom bench had been cased and turned by somebody who knew the work, and Halloran could not make it fit the label. The label gave a bird of the coast. The skin was thinned at the wing butts in the manner of the inland shops, salted rather than pickled, and sewn with a linen thread no coastal shop had bought in twenty years, and the tag was in the curator's own hand.
text_nonnarrative: Objections to dry preparation of skins mostly mistake a question of after-care for a question of method. A dry-prepared skin is stable in a dry room and unstable elsewhere, which is a claim about rooms. The habit of setting one method against another without stating the storage conditions is the real defect of the literature. None of that is an argument for the wet method. Its better contributions give the room first and the bench second.

text_narrative: A salvage party out of the northern shelters brings in forty hides off a store shut for a hundred and ten years. Thirty-nine are green-salted and hard as board. The fortieth is tanned through, supple, and stamped with a mark the shelters have no record of, and the salt on the other thirty-nine is dust dry, and the fortieth is the only hide in the lot with any water left in it.
text_nonnarrative: Reversibility was the mark that divided tanning from preserving, if the two were divided at all. Under salt the conditions for decay were absent and the substance was as it stood; under tan the substance itself was other than it had been, and the conditions were no part of the case. On that second account a tanned hide was not a preserved hide but a different material under one name.

text_narrative: When the long ships were first given leave to carry the dead of other worlds, a vault was cut into the keel of each and filled with spirit to the brim. The rule handed down was that nothing in a vault would change and nothing would be remembered. For eleven crossings this held. On the twelfth the jars in one keel stood clear and full and empty of all but spirit, and the vault was sealed.
text_nonnarrative: Spirit preservation was the maintenance of soft tissue in a bath of dilute alcohol, the bath being both the fixative and the medium of storage. Its stability depended on the concentration of the bath, which was subject to dilution by the water in the tissue itself. Colour was not within the scope of the method. Volume was. The ratio of bath to specimen was therefore the governing figure and was fixed by the water content of the class.

text_narrative: Two hundred years of drift and the wax in the vascular casts has not moved a micron, which is the point of wax, so there is nothing here for Ilinca to write up. Except that the casts are not the casts on the manifest. The manifest gives eleven arterial trees. There are twelve in the case, all injected in one hand, all from one donor code, and the twelfth is the finest work in the collection.
text_nonnarrative: Injection was an argument about what a preparation was for, and the argument was seldom made in the open. A cast was the geometry of a vessel and nothing of its wall, which was a real gain in one dimension and a real loss in another. Those who held for injection had the better of the demonstration and the worse of the record. That did not make the record the more important of the two.

text_narrative: There was a field on the wrong side of a hill where the clamps never froze, and the lord who held it clamped his roots there and nowhere else. His steward built a clamp in the good field one autumn to prove the story wrong. By the turn of the year the good clamp was ice to the heart and the wrong-side clamp was warm to the wrist, and the frost lay a foot deep on both.
text_nonnarrative: The field lay on a north slope at the foot of a long hill, with a spring line across its middle and rising ground on three sides. Clamps stood in two rows along the contour, the lower row on the wetter ground. Soil over the whole field was sand above clay, at a depth of some two feet. The hollow at the western corner was the last part of the field out of shadow.

text_narrative: In the fourteenth winter after the ash the deep store under the ridge was opened on the shortest day and the upper bins were found frosted to the third course. The store had held above freezing for thirteen winters on the heat of the ground alone. The council had the thermometers read hourly for a month, and every reading came back above freezing, and the frost went down a course a week throughout.
text_nonnarrative: Frosted produce means any root showing translucence or a watery separation of the flesh at any depth below the skin, whether or not the store is recorded as having held above freezing. Recorded temperature is evidence and not a definition. Translucence alone is sufficient. Where a bin contains frosted produce, the whole of the course in which that bin stands falls within the term. Nothing in this part affects roots damaged in the lifting.

text_narrative: The second pair are on the line and the ice under them is a hand thicker than the ice under the first pair, which the marker has measured and written down. Odile takes the first stroke. Her saw goes through eleven inches on the down stroke and comes up dry, and the kerf behind it closes white and holds, and the block will not float free although the cut is square all round.
text_nonnarrative: A cut counts only where the kerf is open along its whole length and the block stands free of the field. A block held by a closed kerf is no cut, and the pair holding it have no claim to a second line. Thickness of the field is a condition of the line and not of the cut, so a pair on thick ice are under the requirement of a pair on thin.

text_narrative: Nobody at the county show would enter against Wisniewski's peaches, and the year somebody did the whole class was struck off. She put up nine jars in wire-clip glass, which was not the glass in the schedule, and the steward let them stand. The challenger put up nine in ring glass and had the schedule and lost the table, and the class was gone from the list the following year.
text_nonnarrative: An entry is admissible in the sealed class only where the closure is of the ring pattern named in the schedule, and a wire clip places the jar in the open class whatever its contents. Nine jars are the unit of entry, and a short entry is admissible with the deficiency marked against it. A jar entered in the wrong class is not excluded; it stands in the class its closure gives it.
